related_questions.question: How accurate are COVID rapid tests?

text_blocks.snippet: COVID-19 rapid antigen tests are generally less accurate than PCR tests, particularly in detecting early infections or asymptomatic cases. While they can provide quick results (often within 15 minutes), rapid tests have a higher chance of producing false negative results. If you test positive, it's highly likely you have COVID-19, but a negative result may not be reliable.
snippet_highlighted_words: generally less accurate than PCR tests

list.title: Accuracy:
list.snippet: Rapid antigen tests detect specific proteins (antigens) from the virus, while PCR tests detect the virus's genetic material. PCR tests are generally more sensitive and can detect smaller amounts of the virus, making them more accurate, especially in the early stages of infection or when someone has few symptoms.

list.title: False Negatives:
list.snippet: Rapid tests are more prone to false negatives, meaning they may incorrectly indicate a negative result when the person is actually infected. This is because they may not detect the virus if the viral load is low, or if the test is not performed correctly.

list.title: False Positives:
list.snippet: While less common than false negatives, rapid tests can also produce false positive results, indicating infection when the person is not actually infected. This is less likely with PCR tests.

list.title: When to Use:
list.snippet: If you have symptoms of COVID-19, it's recommended to test immediately, and a PCR test is preferable for greater accuracy, according to OSF HealthCare. If you were exposed to COVID-19 and are asymptomatic, it's best to wait at least five days after exposure before testing, and a PCR test is recommended.

list.title: Repeat Testing:
list.snippet: If you get a negative result on a rapid test, especially if you have symptoms or were exposed, it's recommended to repeat the test to increase the likelihood of detecting an infection.

list.title: Positive Results:
list.snippet: If you test positive on a rapid test, it's important to isolate yourself and take precautions to protect others from potential infection.

related_questions.snippet: Rarely, COVID-19 rapid antigen tests can give false-positive results. False-positive results mean the test results show that you have the virus when you don't. A false-positive is rare and thought to happen in less than 1% of results. In some cases, a false-positive result could be caused by a manufacturing error.

text_blocks.snippet: Rapid antigen tests for COVID-19 are generally good at detecting active infections, especially when a person has a high viral load. However, they are less sensitive than PCR tests, meaning they are more likely to produce a false negative result (indicating a person doesn't have COVID-19 when they actually do).

list.title: How they work:
list.snippet: These tests detect specific proteins (antigens) from the virus, providing results within minutes.

list.title: Accuracy:
list.snippet: They are more accurate when a person has a high viral load, which is typically when they are most infectious.

list.title: False Negatives:
list.snippet: Rapid tests are more prone to false negatives, especially in the early or late stages of infection when viral loads may be lower.

list.title: When to use:
list.snippet: They are useful for quickly identifying people who are likely to be infectious, such as during outbreaks or for screening purposes.

list.title: How they work:
list.snippet: PCR tests detect the virus's genetic material (RNA) and are more sensitive than antigen tests.

list.title: Accuracy:
list.snippet: PCR tests are highly sensitive and accurate, making them the gold standard for detecting COVID-19.

list.title: False Negatives:
list.snippet: PCR tests are less likely to produce false negatives than rapid antigen tests.

list.title: False Positives:
list.snippet: False positive results are also rare with PCR tests.

list.title: When to use:
list.snippet: PCR tests are often used for confirming positive results from rapid antigen tests, for diagnosing cases, and for research purposes.

text_blocks.snippet: In summary: While rapid antigen tests are convenient and provide quick results, PCR tests are more reliable for confirming infection and detecting lower viral loads. Harvard Health advises that if you test positive on a rapid test, you are likely infected, but a negative result, especially if you have symptoms, should be followed up with a PCR test. OSF HealthCare says that PCR tests are preferred for their higher accuracy.
